bibl.title: Working memory capacity of crows and monkeys arises from similar neuronal computations

person.p: the tag layer; a sentence written by the tagger about the paper, always anchored to a quotation but not itself a quotation

span.label: whether the neuronal computation that limits working memory capacity is the same in a bird and a monkey, despite entirely different brain architectures
span.quote: We probed the working memory capacity of crows ( Corvus corone ) in a change detection task, developed for monkeys ( Macaca mulatta ), while we performed extracellular recordings of the prefrontal-like area nidopallium caudolaterale. We found that neuronal encoding and maintenance of information were affected by item load, in a way that is virtually identical to results obtained from monkey prefrontal cortex.

span.label: whether models of working memory capacity built and tested only in mammals describe working memory as such, or only its mammalian implementation
span.quote: As these models are usually conceptualized and tested in an exclusively mammalian context, it remains unclear if they fully capture a general concept of working memory or if they are restricted to the mammalian neocortex. Here, we report that carrion crows and macaque monkeys share divisive normalization as a neuronal computation that is in line with mammalian models. This indicates that computational models of working memory developed in the mammalian cortex can also apply to non-cortical associative brain regions of birds.

span.label: divisive normalization is found in a non-layered avian associative area, with load effects virtually identical to monkey prefrontal cortex
span.quote: We probed the working memory capacity of crows ( Corvus corone ) in a change detection task, developed for monkeys ( Macaca mulatta ), while we performed extracellular recordings of the prefrontal-like area nidopallium caudolaterale. We found that neuronal encoding and maintenance of information were affected by item load, in a way that is virtually identical to results obtained from monkey prefrontal cortex.

span.label: mechanism
span.quote: Here, we report that carrion crows and macaque monkeys share divisive normalization as a neuronal computation that is in line with mammalian models.

span.label: working memory capacity limitation
span.quote: Complex cognition relies on flexible working memory, which is severely limited in its capacity.

span.label: electrophysiology

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: adding a second item normalizes each neuron's firing rate by the pooled response to both colors, shrinking the firing-rate difference between color identities and thereby destroying color information
span.quote: Applied to our context, a consequence of DNR would be a reduced differentiation between two color identities at load 2 because differences in firing rate (for each stimulus by itself) at load 1 would be normalized at load 2 (resulting in information loss, e.g., Figure 2A ).

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: attending one item shifts the weighting of the normalized response toward the attended item, so the same normalization computation can create a color difference where none existed at load 1
span.quote: However, when attention is overtly directed to a specific (preferred or non-preferred) item within the receptive field of a neuron, the DNR computation shifts its weighting of the normalized response toward the response of the attended item ( Reynolds et al., 1999 ; Reynolds and Heeger, 2009 ).

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: recurrent connections confined within a hemisphere let simultaneously present items interfere with each other locally, producing a capacity limit that does not cross hemifields
span.quote: On the neuronal level, recurrent connections between neurons within a hemisphere may reduce item differentiation when multiple items are present simultaneously, creating capacity limitations within the hemisphere ( Matsushima and Tanaka, 2014 ).

span.label: divisive normalization normalizes a neuron's response by the summed activity of a pool when several stimuli are present, which reduces the differentiation between two colors at higher load
span.quote: Divisive normalization is a computational principle that acts upon neurons when presenting multiple stimuli simultaneously, it normalizes neuronal responses by creating ‘a ratio between the response of an individual neuron and the summed activity of a pool of neurons

span.label: and the same computation can produce a GAIN of information, when attention weights the normalization toward one item so that an unequal interaction creates a difference that was not there at load 1
span.quote: We wanted to understand if DNR, the mechanism that we found reduced color information at load 2, could also produce color differentiation. The ‘normalization model of attention’ ( Reynolds and Heeger, 2009 ) incorporates divisive normalization, and can explain how attention can modulate neuronal responses. By attending a preferred (or non-preferred) second colored square in the load 2 condition the neuronal response of a neuron to the target location (i.e., to color A and to color B at the favorite location) might be altered. As a result a difference between color A and B may arise even though each color by itself elicited a similar response.

span.label: recurrent connections within a hemisphere are proposed to reduce item differentiation, with their absence between hemispheres making the two sides independent
span.quote: In contrast, the hemispheric independence we observed would fit a slot-like model, in which the hemispheres as a whole act like discrete slots. A more nuanced version of the slot model (‘slots and averaging’; Zhang and Luck, 2008 ) could also account for graded amounts of information within a limited number of slots ( Fukuda et al., 2010 ; Zhang and Luck, 2008 ), as we found here.

span.label: and graded information on error trials that is not maintained through the delay is read as an insufficient share of a flexible resource rather than a failed slot
span.quote: Furthermore, if there is a flexible resource, in error trials a small but insufficient amount of resource might still be allocated to an item. Indeed, error trial analysis (applying correct trial sub-sampling, see Materials and methods) for the load 2 and 3 conditions further supported this interpretation. The amount of information in the early and late sample phase remained above zero (load 2: early, t (186) = 3.25, p = 0.0014; late, t (186) = 5.33, p < 0.001; load 3: t (156) = 4.21, p < 0.001; Figure 4B asterisks), and was significantly smaller than in correct trials (load 2: late, t (186) = 2.81, p = 0.0055, d = 0.26; load 3: late t (156) = 2.55, p = 0.0117, d = 0.23). Additionally, there was no further maintenance throughout the memory delay at any load ( Figure 4B , PEV at loads 2 and 3 in error trials delay, all non-significant). This indicates that a failure to report which color had changed at higher loads (two and three ipsilateral items) resulted from a smaller amount of information encoding during the sample phase that was not maintained throughout the delay.

span.label: No attentional cueing was used, so the proposed attentional contribution to the load-2 information gain cannot be tested directly.
span.quote: It is important to clarify that, as we did not use any form of attentional cueing in our study, we cannot explicitly test for such an attention effect.

span.label: Aspects of monkey working memory central to the models, notably oscillatory dynamics, were not measured in crows.
span.quote: However, the picture is incomplete since important aspects of monkeys’ WM are still not investigated in crows.

span.label: The data cannot adjudicate between the competing working-memory models that all implement divisive normalization.
span.quote: However, the data we presented cannot carry a definitive conclusion about which of the different models fits best.

span.label: Comparison of the transient activity reported here with synfire-chain/sequence models is only tentative, because small task-design differences change neuronal responses.
span.quote: However, our results can only be compared very cautiously to this (since even small changes in task design significantly alter neuronal responses, e.g., Lara and Wallis, 2014 ).

span.label: attention is offered as the explanation for the information gain, and the study contains no attentional cueing with which to test it
span.quote: It is important to clarify that, as we did not use any form of attentional cueing in our study, we cannot explicitly test for such an attention effect. However, we do know that the animals participating in this study can use attentional cues to enhance their WM

span.label: no neuron showed the persistent delay activity of classical prefrontal studies, and the transient activity found is only cautiously compared with sequence models
span.quote: We cannot report of any neuron that showed persistent activity comparable to those reported by classical WM studies in PFC (e.g., Funahashi et al., 1989 ; Fuster and Alexander, 1971 ), or in NCL ( Diekamp et al., 2002b ; Veit et al., 2014 ; Veit and Nieder, 2013 ). This may be reconcilable with some other contemporary models of WM. One major type of those models implements ‘synfire chains’, where individual neurons fire sequentially (and transiently) to bridge temporal gaps and maintain task relevant contents ( Rajan et al., 2016 ). This has, for example, been reported to be the case in posterior parietal cortex of mice performing a T-maze task that required WM for cued spatial locations to be maintained ( Harvey et al., 2012 ). The transient activity of neurons that we report

span.label: the comparison is cautious precisely because small changes in task design significantly alter neuronal responses
span.quote: However, our results can only be compared very cautiously to this (since even small changes in task design significantly alter neuronal responses, e.g., Lara and Wallis, 2014 ).

span.label: oscillatory dynamics, which mammalian models tie to normalization and competition, are completely unknown in crows
span.quote: However, the picture is incomplete since important aspects of monkeys’ WM are still not investigated in crows. Oscillations of local field potentials are relevant for how information enters WM and how it is maintained ( Miller et al., 2018 ), and have been tied to normalization and competition between items in WM ( Lundqvist et al., 2018b ). Thus, the oscillatory interplay of the layers and different regions of the mammalian neocortex are important fields of research to further our understanding of WM. Such aspects are so far completely unknown in crows and their non-layered associative areas.

span.label: and the data cannot decide between the modern models that all implement normalization
span.quote: Ultimately, our results were in line with different modern models of WM that implement DNR to explain capacity ( Bouchacourt and Buschman, 2019 ; Lundqvist et al., 2016 ; Lundqvist et al., 2011 ; Schneegans et al., 2020 ). However, the data we presented cannot carry a definitive conclusion about which of the different models fits best.

span.label: the change-detection working-memory paradigm and the accompanying capacity models, built and tested on macaques, were imported wholesale to test an avian, non-cortical brain area
span.quote: To investigate the neurophysiology of WM capacity in birds, we adopted a task design developed for monkeys ( Buschman et al., 2011 ) to use it with carrion crows ( Corvus corone ).

span.label: the change-detection task, copied unchanged so that the neuronal results are directly comparable
span.quote: We probed the WM capacity of crows using colored squares, based on the task design of Buschman et al., 2011 . Using the identical task allowed us to directly compare our neuronal results of WM capacity from NCL to results from PFC of monkeys. Task similarity is very important for such cross species comparisons as even small changes in task parameters may introduce substantial differences in neuronal responses, leading to potentially different conclusions.

span.label: divisive normalization and the selectivity-against-interaction regression built to detect it
span.quote: Divisive normalization is a computational principle that acts upon neurons when presenting multiple stimuli simultaneously, it normalizes neuronal responses by creating ‘a ratio between the response of an individual neuron and the summed activity of a pool of neurons

span.label: the normalization model of attention, used to explain how the same computation can create information rather than destroy it
span.quote: We wanted to understand if DNR, the mechanism that we found reduced color information at load 2, could also produce color differentiation. The ‘normalization model of attention’ ( Reynolds and Heeger, 2009 ) incorporates divisive normalization, and can explain how attention can modulate neuronal responses. span.label: the discrete and continuous families of capacity model, imported as the alternatives the data are held against
span.quote: Discrete models’ of WM argue that a fixed number of items can be stored. Once this capacity is reached, an additional item can only be maintained if it replaces a previous item ( Awh et al., 2007 ; Fukuda et al., 2010 ; Luck and Vogel, 1997 ; Vogel and Machizawa, 2004 ; Zhang and Luck, 2008 ). ‘Continuous models’ describe WM as a flexible resource that is allocated to individual items. A minimum amount of this resource has to be allocated to each item for successful retention, thereby resulting in a capacity limit

span.label: information
span.quote: Parallel to the behavioral results and in line with the results from monkeys, we found a strong effect of ipsilateral load on the information maintenance, as there was a sharp drop in information when the load increased from one item to two items ( Figure 4A , blue and yellow curves). The addition of a third item only slightly decreased the maintained information further ( Figure 4A , red curve). The load dependence was much more pronounced during the sample period than during the memory delay where the information remained at a lower elevated level. Notably, the load effect was only present for ipsilateral manipulations. If the number of items on the contralateral side was increased, the information encoded about the colors at the favorite location did not change

span.label: ipsilateral
span.quote: Parallel to the behavioral results and in line with the results from monkeys, we found a strong effect of ipsilateral load on the information maintenance, as there was a sharp drop in information when the load increased from one item to two items ( Figure 4A , blue and yellow curves). The addition of a third item only slightly decreased the maintained information further ( Figure 4A , red curve). The load dependence was much more pronounced during the sample period than during the memory delay where the information remained at a lower elevated level. Notably, the load effect was only present for ipsilateral manipulations. If the number of items on the contralateral side was increased, the information encoded about the colors at the favorite location did not change

span.label: THE TASK IS COPIED SO THAT THE RESULTS CAN BE COMPARED: using the identical task is what allows a direct comparison, because even small changes in task parameters may introduce substantial differences in neuronal responses and lead to different conclusions
span.quote: We probed the WM capacity of crows using colored squares, based on the task design of Buschman et al., 2011 . Using the identical task allowed us to directly compare our neuronal results of WM capacity from NCL to results from PFC of monkeys. Task similarity is very important for such cross species comparisons as even small changes in task parameters may introduce substantial differences in neuronal responses, leading to potentially different conclusions.

span.label: AND THE WORKED EXAMPLE IS IN THE SAME PARAGRAPH: in a similar task, one study found nearly no color information in monkey prefrontal cortex where another found it, so the exact task design may determine what the neurons appear to encode
span.quote: In a task similar to the one used here, Lara and Wallis, 2014 , have found that neurons in the PFC of monkeys encoded nearly no information about color, but instead about location. In their task monkeys had to memorize the color of squares at two locations on a screen, and were again confronted with a colored square at one of the two locations after a delay. The monkeys then had to indicate if the color at that location had changed. Lara and Wallis, 2014 , discuss the absence of color information in the neurons they recorded in relation to the task of Buschman et al., 2011 , who like us, did find color information. In brief, the exact task design may determine the neuronal encoding of task relevant information

span.label: A MODEL'S SCOPE IS TESTED BY MOVING IT OFF THE SUBSTRATE IT WAS BUILT ON: the model rests solely on monkey electrophysiology and is thus implicitly tied to the layered columns of the neocortex, and it fits a non-layered avian area too
span.quote: The WM model of Bouchacourt and Buschman, 2019 , is based solely on data from monkey electrophysiology, and thus implicitly tied to the layered columns of the neocortex. The results we report here show that the model also fits the neurophysiology of WM in crows.

span.label: ONE COMPUTATION, TWO OPPOSITE OUTCOMES, AND THE PAPER SAYS SO: the same normalization that destroys information in one subpopulation creates it in another, which may appear counter-intuitive and contradictory
span.quote: This may appear counter-intuitive and contradictory, considering that the same process is also responsible for the loss of information. However, when attention is overtly directed to a specific (preferred or non-preferred) item within the receptive field of a neuron, the DNR computation shifts its weighting of the normalized response toward the response of the attended item ( Reynolds et al., 1999 ; Reynolds and Heeger, 2009 ). This weighted normalization can produce a difference in the neuronal response to both color identities at load 2, even if the neuronal response was non-informative at load 1.

span.label: and the whole theoretical claim reduces to one number - a regression slope of about 0.5 means both items influence the response equally, which is what normalization predicts
span.quote: If DNR was present, this influence to suppress or enhance neuronal responses should be an even mixture at the population level, resulting in a significant regression between SE and SI with a slope of around 0.5

span.label: THE CRITERION DETERMINES THE POPULATION FOUND: more than half the significant delay neurons were significant only at load 2 or load 3, so testing at load 1 alone would have missed them
span.quote: For the memory delay, more than half of the significant neurons we detected were only significant for either load 2 or load 3, compared to only 36% of neurons that were significant at load 1 ( Figure 3C middle). By including the higher loads in our analysis, we found a total of 249 (68.78%) sample neurons and 94 (25.97%) delay neurons.

span.label: and the neurons that gain information at higher load were found only because the selection was widened, not because they were predicted
span.quote: Further inspection of individual neuronal activity revealed, however, that a substantial number of neurons responded differently. Instead of losing information at higher loads, many neurons gained information (e.g., Figure 2B , Figure 2—figure supplement 2 ). Thus, we additionally performed the permutation testing for loads 2 and 3 to determine which neurons had significant information (see Materials and methods). We found that many of the neurons that did not have significant information at load 1 did have significant information at load 2 and load 3

span.label: THE DATA FIT BOTH RIVAL FAMILIES IN DIFFERENT RESPECTS: graded within-hemifield allocation fits a continuous resource, hemispheric independence fits discrete slots, and a nuanced slots-and-averaging model accommodates both
span.quote: In contrast, the hemispheric independence we observed would fit a slot-like model, in which the hemispheres as a whole act like discrete slots. A more nuanced version of the slot model (‘slots and averaging’; Zhang and Luck, 2008 ) could also account for graded amounts of information within a limited number of slots ( Fukuda et al., 2010 ; Zhang and Luck, 2008 ), as we found here.

span.label: with the paper declining to choose - the data cannot carry a definitive conclusion about which model fits best
span.quote: Ultimately, our results were in line with different modern models of WM that implement DNR to explain capacity ( Bouchacourt and Buschman, 2019 ; Lundqvist et al., 2016 ; Lundqvist et al., 2011 ; Schneegans et al., 2020 ). However, the data we presented cannot carry a definitive conclusion about which of the different models fits best.

span.label: SHARED COMPUTATION ACROSS UNSHARED ARCHITECTURE IS THE POINT: differently organised areas produce strikingly similar physiological responses, which is read as convergent evolution onto the same basic mechanisms and the same limits
span.quote: Together, all these facets of crow WM capacity suggest that the different intricate neuronal architectures that carry out the computations in monkeys and crows have likely been shaped by convergent evolution – into systems that yield similar cognitive performances. The systems may share the same basic mechanisms and thus limitations.

span.label: replicates → Balakhonov and Rose, 2017 (behavioural crow WM capacity) and Buschman et al., 2011 (primate WM capacity)
span.quote: These observations are very similar to observations made in primates ( Buschman et al., 2011 ) and fully reproduce our earlier behavioral findings ( Balakhonov and Rose, 2017 ).

span.quote: To compare our results to the results obtained in monkeys we also applied the method of Buschman et al., 2011 for testing the ipsilateral load effect during the sample and delay phase, by splitting each phase into an early and a late portion (first and second 400 ms of the sample, and first and second 500 ms for the delay).

A neuron called non-informative carries information - about occupancy, not identity. The label is relative to the feature the analysis asked about. Q-476. · strength of the relation: 1 — and the non-informative neurons' smaller slope is read as their being informative about WHETHER a color was at their favourite location rather than which
span.quote: Non-informative sample neurons had a fitted slope of 0.38 ( R 2 adj = 0.16, F (1,1366) = 258.08, p < 0.001), significantly smaller than 0.5 (CI = [0.33 0.42]). Delay neurons had a slope of 0.40, also significantly smaller than 0.5 ( R 2 adj = 0.13, F (1,1366) = 197.51, p < .001, CI = [0.35 0.46]).
